# QR Symbology Architecture

Design record for supporting multiple QR symbologies in one library: Standard QR (ISO/IEC 18004), Micro QR (ISO/IEC 18004) and rMQR (ISO/IEC 23941). This document defines how the codebase is organized, so that adding one symbology does not destabilize the others. Implementation details live in code comments next to the code.

---

## What

### Symbology status

| Symbology | Standard | Encode | Matrix decode | Image decode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard QR (versions 1–40) | ISO/IEC 18004 | Shipped | Shipped | Shipped (Tier 1–2) |
| Micro QR (M1–M4) | ISO/IEC 18004 | Shipped | Shipped | Shipped (Tier 1–2, conservative measured envelope) |
| rMQR (R7x43–R17x139) | ISO/IEC 23941 | Encode + render done (Phase 5, encoder MVT met; not yet released) | Done (Phase 6, decoder MVT matrix rows met; not yet released) | Done (Phase 7, Tier 1–2, measured envelope incl. keystone up to 4 % on R17x139; not yet released) |

### Document set

The specs are one set of files per symbology, plus this cross-cutting record. The [documentation index](../README.md) lists the files. Structure and naming rules are in [docs_authoring_guidelines.md](../docs_authoring_guidelines.md). A new symbology copies the section skeleton of the Standard QR document of the same type.

### Internal organization

Internals are split into shared primitives and per-symbology pipelines.

**Shared primitives** (`Internals`, `Internals.BinaryEncoders`, `Internals.BinaryDecoders`, `Internals.ImageDecoders`) hold the knowledge that is identical across all three symbologies:

| Component | Why it is shared |
|---|---|
| `GaloisField`, `Polynom`, `EccBinaryEncoder`, `EccBinaryDecoder` | All three symbologies use Reed-Solomon over GF(256) with the same primitive polynomial (0x11D) |
| `BitWriter`, `BitReader` | Bit-stream packing is symbology-independent |
| `ModuleBitPacker` | The Micro QR and rMQR data models convert between one byte per module and MSB-first packed bits (`SetCoreData` / `GetCoreData`), and the conversion is the same for both. Standard QR's `QRCodeData` keeps its own (frozen) storage kernel |
| `ECCInfo` | RS block structure (data codewords, ECC per block, up to two block groups) describes all three symbologies |
| `BinaryInterleaver` | Interleaving the blocks' data codewords, then their ECC codewords, depends only on the `ECCInfo` block structure. Standard QR and rMQR interleave identically (Micro QR has one block). It moved from `Internals.StandardQR` to `Internals.BinaryEncoders` when rMQR became its second consumer (rMQR Phase 5.4). The only symbology-specific input, the remainder-bit count, is passed in by the caller |
| `EccBlockDecoder` | The Reed-Solomon block stage of the matrix decoders. It deinterleaves the stream into its blocks (the exact inverse of `BinaryInterleaver`), corrects each block up to a capacity the symbology passes in, and gathers the data in block order. Standard QR and rMQR run it. Micro QR has one block and a half codeword, and corrects it itself. Until 2026-09-29 Standard QR and rMQR each had their own copy of the stage, rMQR's as a fused loop of its own. Sharing it changed no read and no status, and rMQR's loop, put back, measured 1.6 to 2.8 % slower than the shared stage on a matrix with errors. A stream of a single block is already in block order, so it is corrected in place, without the deinterleave and the copy back (2026-10-01). Of rMQR's 64 versions and levels, 29 have a single block; of Standard QR's 160, 12 do, all at versions 1 to 5 |
| `EncodingMode`, `TextAnalyzer`, `CharacterSets` | The mode alphabets (the Numeric, Alphanumeric and Byte character classes, and the alphanumeric encoding values) are shared. Only the indicator widths and which modes are legal differ per symbology. `EncodingMode` also has a Kanji member, whose cells come from the shared `ShiftJisKanjiReverseTable`. The analysis selects Kanji for an eligible text when the caller sets `AllowKanji` |
| `SegmentDecoders` | The segment payload bit groups (numeric 10/7/4, alphanumeric 11/6, byte 8·count), the byte-charset heuristics (UTF-8 validation, BOM, Latin-1 widening) and the ECI designator reader are identical across symbologies. The ECI designator reader moved out of `QRBinaryDecoder` when rMQR became its second consumer (Phase 6). The mode and count indicator framing differs per symbology, so it stays in each symbology's bitstream decoder. The shared parts moved out of `QRBinaryDecoder` in Phase 3, when the second consumer appeared |
| `LuminanceConverter`, `PixelLayout`, `PerspectiveTransform` | Image preprocessing and geometry are symbology-independent. The first-party image adapter hands its pixels to the luminance kernels; that is the seam described under the package seam below |
| `Point`, `Rectangle` | Plain geometry types |
| `ModuleRunScanner`, `ModuleRunEnumerator<TView>` | Merging dark modules into horizontal runs depends only on the `IModuleMatrixView` shape, not on the symbology. One implementation serves both the renderer's merged-run drawing path and the public `GetModuleRectangles` on all three data types. So for an unstyled symbol, the geometry the public API reports is, by construction, the geometry the renderer draws. A styled symbol draws each finder as one pattern instead, and `GetModuleRectangles` still reports it as the merged runs of its modules |

**Per-symbology pipelines** (`Internals.StandardQR`, later `Internals.MicroQR`, `Internals.RmQR`) hold the knowledge specific to one symbol format:

- Capacity / ECC / interleaving tables and version selection
- Mode indicator and character-count indicator widths
- Format (and version) information encoding and decoding
- Function pattern layout, data module placement, mask patterns and mask scoring
- Symbol detection and sampling in images

Dependency rule: shared code never references a symbology namespace, and symbology namespaces never reference each other. Each symbology pipeline is built from the shared primitives.

`SymbologyDependencyTest` enforces the rule on the library's build for every target framework. Code under a framework's `#if` is therefore checked in the build where it compiles. Code that depends on the configuration (`#if DEBUG`, and a call to a `[Conditional("DEBUG")]` method such as `Debug.Assert`) is checked only in the configuration the tests run in, which is Release on CI. A build older than a source file of the library is not checked: its case is skipped, or fails on CI.

The test fails on any reference from a type in an internal namespace to a type of another symbology, or of a namespace below one, however the source spelled it (a `using` of any kind, a global import, a linked file). The reference can be a base type or interface, a signature, a local, a catch type, a generic constraint, an attribute or a type named in its arguments, or a member or type named in a method's code. Probe types in the test assembly confirm that the test catches each of these kinds, except a pinned local and a call through a function pointer, which only unsafe code makes.

Some uses compile to no reference: a constant (an enum member among them) or a `nameof`. A source check covers those. It reads each internal file's code, with comments and `#if false` branches removed, and looks for another symbology's namespace spelled out, a `using` of it, or a type qualified by its name. A constant reached by a spelling the check does not know passes.

Existing Standard QR code moves under `Internals.StandardQR` unchanged. No change to behavior or algorithms accompanies the move.

Two detection primitives were moved from `Internals.StandardQR` to the shared `Internals.ImageDecoders` namespace when Micro QR image detection (Phase 4b) became their second consumer, which is exactly the trigger this document prescribed:

- `Binarizer`, generic binarization (moved out of `QRImageDecoder`). The histogram is counted once per image. A 256-bit tier, an ARM64 tier and a 128-bit tier count a block's two extreme values in registers, and the ARM64 tier spreads dense blocks over four sub-histograms; where no vector is accelerated, a scalar walk counts it. The threshold search and the grey levels use only the histogram. The levels also give the luminance at which an edge is located: halfway between them, whether or not the image has grey pixels. The inverted retry that every image decoder makes does not count the negative image. It mirrors the first polarity's bins and searches the threshold again on them, because two values with nothing between them tie at every split, and `256 - threshold` is a different threshold exactly on a rendered symbol. All four tiers are checked to produce the same bin counts. The decisions and measurements are in [standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md)
- `FinderPatternFinder`, the 1:1:3:1:1 run-ratio scan and its cross-checks. Micro QR and rMQR use the same finder pattern shape (one finder instead of three) through `FindCandidates`. It returns the cross-checked candidates, and the decoder chooses how many of them to decode (a bounded number). Micro QR and rMQR both take them in the order `RankByConfirmation` gives, most confirmed first. Standard QR keeps its best-three selection in `TryFind`. Runs that miss the ratio by less than 1.5 px on each of the five are measured again from grey levels (`GreyLevels`, taken from the threshold's own histogram) before they are refused. This is what reads anti-aliased edges at about 2 px/module.
  - Each cross-check line must meet the ratio on its own. A column may be longer or shorter than its row by as much as a finder in perspective is drawn (5/12 to 12/5), but more than 40 % away from the row's length only when the rising diagonal also reads. This finds the finder that a strong keystone stretches, in all three symbologies. On 540 two-level noise images it gives 30 more candidates (474 against 444), and the same 60 of them yield a triple. The single-finder decoders' failures took 2 to 7 % longer (rMQR noise, a turned Micro QR); this was not traced further.
  - A cross-check line that the ratio refuses is measured again by the distances between its edges of the same polarity (`IsFinderRatioByLikeEdges`). Those distances survive a ring printed or read too thick or too thin. This second measurement is accepted only within the row's own 40 %, with the row's shift sign, and with the rising diagonal checked too. Its cost is in [standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md#image-detection-and-sampling), and what it reads is in each decoder's image envelope
- `LocalBinarizer`, a regional binarization: 8 × 8 blocks, with each pixel compared against the mean black point of the 5 × 5 blocks around its own. It is the regional pass of every image decoder ([Image decode passes](#image-decode-passes)). `RegionalRetry` runs its two polarities, each binarized from its own pixels, so the three decoders share the order and the skips. It reads symbols under a lighting gradient. Why it is an added attempt rather than a replacement is in [standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md#image-detection-and-sampling)
- `ImageDecodePasses`, the image decode passes themselves ([Image decode passes](#image-decode-passes)). It is one sequence and one set of rules for the three image decoders. Each decoder supplies its symbol pass as a struct (`ISymbolPass`), so the calls stay direct. The midpoint pass is switched on by that struct, and is off for Standard QR. Until 2026-09-29 each decoder ran its own copy of the sequence, and Micro QR's and rMQR's copies were the same line for line. Moving them changed no read and no status over the image decode sweep and the real-image corpus
- `ImageView`, an image as one pass reads it: pixels, size, threshold, grey levels and the level at which an edge is located. The image decoders' stages pass it down as one argument, where they used to take five or six. The stages that measure (finder sizes, grids, samplers) still take the pieces they read, so each one states what it reads, and a test can call it alone. It was added on 2026-09-29, when stages in Standard QR's search took up to 16 parameters each to carry the image.
- `CandidateScan`, the scan of the two decoders that read around a single finder, Micro QR and rMQR. It covers which candidates are decoded, what ends a candidate and the scan, and what is reported ([single-finder candidate scan](#single-finder-candidate-scan)). Each decoder supplies its decode of one candidate as a struct (`ICandidateDecoder`), so the calls stay direct. It was added on 2026-10-01; until then each decoder had its own copy, the same line for line
- `GridRead`, the decode of a sampled grid and its re-read by coverage in Micro QR and rMQR, with the gate they share and each decoder's own condition ([single-finder candidate scan](#single-finder-candidate-scan)). Each decoder supplies its grid as a struct (`IGridRead`). It was added on 2026-10-01; until then each decoder had its own gate and re-read
- `SymbolGeometry`, where a symbol that was read lies in the image. It holds the corners of the mapping that decoded the symbol (`SymbolCorners`), which every image decoder reports with a successful read. It also tests whether a point lies inside those corners (`Contains`, `AnyContains`). The Micro QR and rMQR scans apply that test to later candidates after a read that does not fit the destination ([single-finder candidate scan](#single-finder-candidate-scan))
- `AttemptStatus` and `SearchResult`, how the image decoders interpret a decode attempt's status, and which result a search of many attempts reports.
  - The status classes are defined once. A read, or a read too long for the destination, is terminal. A verdict on the content settles the symbol. A grid that got past its format information is worth refining. How far an attempt got is also defined once.
  - A search reports its failure by one of two rules. Standard QR reports, at each level of its search, the main path's attempt (the one it would make if it had no other), unless another attempt settles. Micro QR and rMQR report the failure that went furthest, since they try many grids of one finder and none of them comes first.
  - Standard QR keeps its own rule because its format word does not encode the version. A grid sampled at a guessed dimension reads near-random bits in the format area. About half of all 15-bit words lie within three bits of a valid word, so such a grid gets past the format information by chance, then fails at Reed-Solomon with the version of its own dimension. When Standard QR was switched to the furthest failure on 2026-09-30 as a trial, 51 of 80 symbols with their format information destroyed reported `DataUncorrectable` one version too small, where they had reported `FormatInformationInvalid` with their own version. No read changed. Micro QR's format word encodes the symbol, and rMQR's the version, so in those a grid of a size other than the one the word gives is refused at the format information.
  - Each decoder still decides where its own search stops. A terminal result ends the passes in all three. Inside a pass, Standard QR stops at a settled result. Micro QR's and rMQR's scans stop at a read. They also stop at a read too long for the destination, but only once the other candidates of its finder scan have run, since another symbol in the image may read ([single-finder candidate scan](#single-finder-candidate-scan)).
  - Standard QR creates a level's result only at the level's first attempt that does not settle. It returns a settled attempt as it is, which is what either rule reports when only unsettled attempts came before it. On the WebAssembly interpreter every result operation is a call. Created ahead of each level, the results cost a version 6 read at 4 px/module about 6 µs of 136, and nothing measurable when compiled (2026-10-01).
  - Micro QR's and rMQR's rules for a finder candidate, including a read that does not fit the destination, are in [single-finder candidate scan](#single-finder-candidate-scan).
  - Until 2026-09-29 each decoder had its own copy of these, and the furthest-failure ranking existed twice.
- Not shared, on purpose: the mirror retry. A mirrored capture has the same finders, with its data transposed. The three decoders read it in three ways, each for a reason:
  - Standard QR transposes its sampled grid in place, since its matrix level reads the modules two at a time along the placement runs, which a transposed view would not keep contiguous.
  - Micro QR reads its grid through a transposed view, since its matrix level reads every module through one; one helper does it for every grid.
  - rMQR samples again with the frame's axes swapped, since a transposed rMQR grid is no rMQR grid.
- `ModuleBoundaryReader`, which reads the grid of a crisp axis-aligned symbol below 1.75 px/module as a table of module boundaries, taken from the timing patterns and the finder's own lines instead of from a fitted transform. Each symbology says where its timing lines run and how they end: at a far finder for Standard QR, and at the quiet zone for Micro QR and rMQR, with rMQR's three-module alignment and corner runs allowed on the line
- `ConcentricCentroid`, which finds a concentric pattern's centre as the centroid of the darkness of its centre square, in a window along the symbol's axes that ends inside the light ring. That is accurate to a fraction of a pixel, where thresholded runs give half a pixel. It needs the grey levels: on a two-level image it leaves the centre as it is. It refines the three Standard QR finders and Standard QR's alignment patterns and mesh nodes, the Micro QR finder, and the rMQR finder and sub-finder
- `PerspectiveGridSampler`, which reads a square module grid through one projective transform, comparing the pixel at each module centre against the threshold. It has 256-bit and 128-bit tiers. It samples Standard QR's four-point, parallelogram and finders' frame grids, and Micro QR's perspective search. Until 2026-09-29 it was `QRImageDecoder.SampleGrid`, and Micro QR called it there, against the dependency rule. `SymbologyDependencyTest` now enforces the rule over the built library and the source. rMQR keeps its own sampler, since its grid is not square and has an affine tier
- `LuminanceSampler`, luminance interpolated between pixel centres, for the coverage reading. The first reading compares one pixel against the global threshold. On an image with grey levels, a grid that failed is read again, comparing each module's centre against the midpoint of the two levels, and it is decoded again only when that changes a module. The grids read again this way are Standard QR's global grid, a Micro QR grid that read its format word exactly, and an rMQR grid that read its format information
- `FinderAxisEstimator`, which does two things:
  - It measures the finder-local module scale for all three symbologies. It uses dark-light-dark runs that pair edges of the same polarity, so ink spread and erosion do not change the scale. For Standard QR on an image with grey levels, it pairs sub-pixel edges the same way, located where the luminance interpolated along the line crosses halfway between the two levels. That is fine enough to measure how the module size changes along a finder line under perspective.
  - It recovers a single finder's axes for Micro QR and rMQR: an axis fitted to a 90-direction sweep, then the sweep's separated minima.
  - It moved out of the Micro QR image decoder when rMQR image detection (Phase 7) became its second consumer, and the Standard QR finder-to-finder measurement was merged into it in 2026-09
- `FinderOutline`, which measures a 7 × 7 finder's own frame, shear included, from the inner edges of its light ring, whereas the angular sweep gives square frames. rMQR measures a finder in strong perspective with it. `ProjectiveFit` is the least-squares homography from point correspondences, accumulated as moments with nothing stored. It fits the perimeter rMQR traces ([rmqr-decoder.md](rmqr-decoder.md)), and places the Standard QR mesh nodes for versions 7 to 13 that are not searched or not found ([standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md#piecewise-mesh-version-7)). The image side is moved and scaled to unit size first, because raw pixel sums lose the fit from about 4,000 px out

### Image decode passes

The three image decoders read an image in the same sequence of passes, run by one shared driver (`ImageDecodePasses`). Only Micro QR and rMQR have the last pass, the midpoint pass. Each pass sets how the image is read, then runs the symbology's own pipeline on it. The global and midpoint passes set a threshold on the luminance; the regional pass instead produces an image binarized region by region. A pass runs only when the passes before it read nothing, and the rules below say which results end the sequence early. The per-symbology pipelines are drawn in the spec-to-code maps: [Standard QR](standardqr-spec-map.md#decoding-pipeline), [Micro QR](microqr-spec-map.md#image-detection-and-sampling), [rMQR](rmqr-spec-map.md#image-detection-and-sampling).

```
Luminance ──> histogram, counted once
├─ Global, positive   Otsu threshold ──> symbol pass
├─ Global, negative   the image inverted; Otsu threshold of the mirrored histogram ──> symbol pass
├─ Regional           each pixel against the mean black point of the blocks around its own,
│                     positive then negative ──> symbol pass each
└─ Midpoint           Micro QR and rMQR, for each polarity whose global pass found no finder candidate:
                      halfway between its two grey levels ──> full finder sweep ──> symbology pipeline

Symbol pass
├─ Standard QR        finder triple ──> symbology pipeline
│                     the triple comes from a strided row scan, which also scans the rows it skipped when it
│                     selects no triple, or selects a doubtful one after setting once-seen candidates aside
└─ Micro QR, rMQR     strided finder scan ──> symbology pipeline
                      nothing read: full finder sweep ──> symbology pipeline
```

- The rules count attempts. Each global pass is one symbol pass. The regional pass runs one symbol pass per polarity, and the midpoint pass one full sweep per polarity that qualifies; in both, the positive goes first.
- A read ends the sequence: nothing runs after the attempt that made it. A read here includes text that was decoded but did not fit the destination.
- A verdict on the content (`UnmappedCharacter`, `UnsupportedContent`) means the symbol was seen, and it ends the sequence the same way. There are two exceptions:
  - After a verdict from the global positive pass, the global negative pass still runs, and a read there wins.
  - A verdict from the strided scan of a Micro QR or rMQR symbol pass does not skip that pass's full sweep, which can find another symbol that reads.
- The full sweep of a Micro QR or rMQR symbol pass does not decode a candidate equal to one that its strided scan already decoded without settling, because the same position and module size, image and threshold give the same outcome. Equal means equal to the bit. The sweep's estimate of a finder is an average over more rows, so it can differ from the strided one, and such a candidate is decoded again. The sweep still tries only its own first eight, so a skipped one is not replaced by the ninth. When the strided scan settled on a verdict, nothing is skipped.
- When one attempt reaches more than one result, the symbology's own rule decides which it reports (see its map).
- The regional pass is skipped when a side of the image is 32 px or less, which leaves too few blocks for one neighbourhood, or when the image holds only 0 and 255. Within the pass, a polarity is not decoded when its binarization leaves every pixel in the class its global threshold gave it.
- The regional pass reads an image with only two levels, so it has no grey levels, and no stage that needs them runs in it.
- The midpoint pass needs grey levels, and it is skipped when the midpoint equals the global threshold.
- The global threshold can land inside a wide, noisy background. With the levels squeezed to 100-170, ±24 of noise, and the symbol a small part of the image, Otsu lands near 165, inside the light background. In 65 of 65 such failures the finder was never a candidate (measured on rMQR, 2026-09-28; every symbology uses this threshold).
- When no pass reads the symbol or gives a verdict, the result carries the global positive pass's diagnostics. For Micro QR and rMQR, those are the diagnostics of its strided scan.

Why the passes are ordered this way:
- Every pass after the first runs only on an image the passes before it failed to read. An image the global threshold reads therefore pays for nothing else, and the buffer for the inverted image is rented only after that failure.
- The negative needs no second count, because its histogram is the positive's mirrored (`Binarizer` above).
- A read too long for the destination ends the sequence as a read does. Measured with the inverted and regional passes run after it, a call one character short cost 2.15 times a sized one at the median on the 577 Micro QR `destination` renders, and 2.46 times on the 600 rMQR renders. At worst it cost up to 93 and 72 times respectively (2026-10-02).
- The regional pass is an added attempt, not a replacement for the global threshold ([standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md#image-detection-and-sampling)).
- A verdict ends only what could not change the answer. A rule stated for one symbol has to hold for the whole image. Stopping a Micro QR or rMQR search at a verdict would also stop it for every other symbol in the image. A verdict from the strided scan that skipped the full sweep lost 20 to 24 readable neighbours in about 490 pairs of an unmapped symbol beside a readable low-density one. The price is that a symbol holding an unmapped Kanji cell cost 2 to 19 ms, against microseconds for a mappable one (2026-09-23, before the failure-path work made those searches faster).
- The midpoint pass is for a finder the global threshold cannot see. Edge greys pull that threshold toward light, and a blurred finder's light ring can then keep too few pixels above it. Halfway between the two levels, the ring is read at its full width. The pass runs last, so a symbol the regional pass reads never pays for it. Since the cross-checks also measure between edges of the same polarity, most such finders are found at the global threshold. Among bilinear upscales of every version at 2 to 3.2 px/module, only Micro QR M1 and rMQR R7x43 and R7x77 still needed it. Standard QR has no midpoint pass. Its sweep read 4,799 of 4,800 bilinear renders at 2 to 3.5 px/module without one, and the one left was also unread before the passes were shared (2026-09-29). Adding the pass would be an accuracy change of its own, measured by the sweep, for an input class that needs it.
- The finder search widens in two different ways because the trigger to widen has to be a question about the symbol. Standard QR's search can ask one itself: did the strided rows give it a triple that is not in doubt? A single-finder scan cannot ask anything like that, so the Micro QR and rMQR decoders ask instead whether the strided scan read the symbol ([rmqr-decoder.md](rmqr-decoder.md#decisions), finder candidate scan).

### Single-finder candidate scan

Micro QR and rMQR read around a single finder. They share how its candidates are scanned (`CandidateScan`), and how a grid that may be read again by coverage is read (`GridRead`). Each decoder supplies only what is its own, on a struct: its decode of one candidate (`ICandidateDecoder`) and its grids (`IGridRead`). One test per rule checks both decoders (`DestinationContractTest`, through the public `TryDecodeImage`). `CandidateScanTest` and `GridReadTest` check the shared code with scripted decoders and grids.

```
Symbol pass (Micro QR, rMQR)
├─ Strided finder scan ──> ranked candidates, most confirmed first ──> the first ones
│  └─ Each, unless a read that did not fit lies around it
│     └─ A result of its own ──> the decoder's grids, those it reads again by coverage through GridRead
│        ──> ends at a terminal result
└─ Neither a read nor a read too long: full finder sweep, the same way, less any candidate equal to one
   the strided scan tried, unless that scan settled on a verdict

GridRead: the grid's decode ──> on an image with grey levels, a grid past its format information that neither
          read nor read too long for the destination, and that the decoder's own condition allows,
          read again by coverage ──> decoded again only when a module changed; the further of the two returned
A read ends the scan. A read too long for the destination ends its candidate, keeps its corners for the skip,
and ends the scan once the other candidates of its finder scan have run. Otherwise each finder scan reports the
result that went furthest, its corners stripped, and the scan the sweep's if it settled, else the strided scan's
```

**The scan**
- **The first eight candidates, most confirmed first.** A false hit ranks behind, since repeated row hits separate a finder from texture. A candidate skipped is not replaced by the next in rank.
- **A read ends the scan.** Another symbol in the image may read, so after a failure, a verdict on the content or a read too long for the destination, the other candidates of that finder scan still run.
- **After a read too long for the destination, the full sweep does not run.** A sized call stops at that symbol as a read, so a call that probes for the destination's size costs what a sized one does. Measured with the sweep run after it, a call one character short cost about 1.9 times a sized one at the median on the 577 Micro QR `destination` renders, and 1.6 times on the 600 rMQR renders (2026-10-01). The reads this rule costs are a residual (below).
- **A read too long for the destination ends its candidate.** The candidate's grids are tried in the same order whatever the destination, so that read is the one a sized call returns, if its content allows (below). A later grid of the candidate could only read something else, at up to hundreds of times the cost:
  - before this rule, sizing probes cost rMQR 250 to 500 times a sized call (73 ms against 0.2 ms at R13x99);
  - until 2026-09-30, on 577 Micro QR renders a destination one character short cost 105 times a sized call at the median and up to 1,095 times. Once the candidate stopped there, it cost 1.00 times at the median and at most 5.8.
- **Each candidate keeps a result of its own.** While the candidates shared the scan's result, a read that did not fit on one candidate ended each later candidate at its first frame that read a format copy. A second symbol that fits was then missed, unless that frame read it.
- **A later candidate inside a symbol that read but did not fit is skipped.**
  - Symbols do not overlap, so such a candidate is a finder-like pattern in that symbol's own data.
  - Searched in full after the read, it cost rMQR about 86 times a sized call through a frame's grid, 40 through the module boundaries and 8.5 through the coverage re-read, and Micro QR 32 to 39 times (per-call medians in one run of the full suite, 2026-10-02).
  - With the skip, nine runs of the `destination` sets gave a median of 1.00, a 95th percentile of 1.01 to 1.03, and a worst case that varied from 1.02 to 1.46, from a different render each run (2026-10-01 and 02).
  - The skip keeps the corners of every read that did not fit, not only the first.
- **The corners go with a read only.** A read that did not fit keeps them until the scan has used them. Every result other than a read is reported without them, so the public `Corners` is empty on a failure.
- **The report is the result that went furthest, the first on a tie** (`SearchResult`), in each finder scan. A read too long for the destination ranks above a verdict on the content, since a larger destination reads that symbol, while a verdict holds at any size. When the two ranked equal, keeping the first made the report depend on the candidates' order.
- **Across the two finder scans, the sweep's result is reported if it settled, and the strided scan's if not.** When both fail, the strided scan's failure is reported: those are the diagnostics a caller saw before the sweep existed. This holds even where the sweep's failure went further.
- **This rests on the segment decoders' order.** They check the declared character count against the remaining bits before they check the caller's buffer, so a malformed count cannot pass for a short buffer. They check the content after the buffer, which leaves a residual (below).

**The grid read**
- A grid is read again by coverage when all of these hold:
  - the image has grey levels;
  - the grid got past its format information;
  - it neither read nor read too long for the destination;
  - the decoder's own condition holds.
- A re-read is decoded only when it changes a module, and the further of the two decodes is returned.
- A grid is never read again after a read, or after a read too long for the destination. On a real image, the same grid read again gives the same text. On an image crafted to read another text by coverage, a call too short for the first text got the other text back as a success, which a sized call never returns.
  - rMQR alone still made that re-read until 2026-10-01.
  - On upright renders upscaled bilinearly it cost up to 2.8 times a sized call (R13x99 and R17x139 at 2 to 2.5 px/module). Over the 585 renders, the mean went from 1.05 to 1.00 times.
- The decoders' own conditions:
  - **Micro QR:** an orientation that got past its format information read that word exactly. Its single format copy lets 7 to 21 % of random grids past, depending on the version; texture reads a word within 3 bits about half the time, and exactly about 1 in 1,000.
  - **rMQR:** budget left. Its two copies let about 1.5 % of random grids past.

**What stays each decoder's**
- Its grid search: Micro QR's sizes, timing frame, module boundaries, arbitrary orientation and scale and perspective searches; rMQR's frames, outline, format copies, sub-finder, perimeter trace and perspective search.
- Which grids are read again: Micro QR's per-size and search grids, but not its timing frame or module-boundary table; every grid rMQR samples through a transform.
- Its mirror retry, three ways ([internal organization](#internal-organization)).
- Its budget. The two are tuned to measured envelopes in different units, so they are not unified; revisit only with a measured reason:
  - Micro QR: 10,000 decodes on the arbitrary-orientation path, two per grid, with the re-read not counted, which leaves room for one complete frame.
  - rMQR: 256 decodes per candidate across all its frames, counting a re-read whether or not it decodes. `GridRead` reports a re-read, so each decoder charges its budget as it always did.
- Standard QR uses neither: its triple and mesh paths and its main-path report rule (`SearchResult`, above) are its own. Revisit only if `GridRead` can take Standard QR's coverage re-read without changing that rule.

**How the code is shaped**
- **The scratch.** The scan holds one module buffer for its candidates, and none when it found no candidate. Micro QR's 289 B come from the stack, and rMQR's 2,363 B are rented, since a scan holds one buffer at a time ([allocation contract](#allocation-contract)). The small tables are set up inside each candidate's decode.
  - A struct cannot hold a span unless it is a `ref struct`. netstandard2.0 cannot pass a ref struct as a generic argument, and has no static abstract members. So the decoder's part is instance members on a struct, as in `ImageDecodePasses`.
- **The corners.** The scan reads and strips them through the decoder's struct, not through an interface on the public diagnostic records, which would change public types to serve internals.
- **The grid's results.** A decoder's grid holds what its last decode found, which is why `GridRead` takes it by `ref`. Micro QR's condition needs each orientation's result, and it is still checked only once the shared conditions hold.
- **Behaviour unchanged.** Moving the scan and the grid read changed no read and no status over the image decode sweeps (byte-identical result files), this library's columns of the real-image corpus and the short-destination sets. The image decode benchmarks stayed within their error bars (2026-10-01).

**How it is held**
- Planted faults ([`tools/mutants/single-finder-candidate-scan.tsv`](../../../tools/mutants/single-finder-candidate-scan.tsv), run by `tools/mutation_check.cs`, each against the full suite, 2026-10-02). There are 51 of them:
  - one at each place a decoder returns on a terminal result, the fault letting it go on: 9 in `MicroQRImageDecoder`, 13 in `RmQRImageDecoder`;
  - the scan's, the grid read's and the corners' rules;
  - each decoder's coverage condition and rMQR's budget.

  46 are caught: the scan's rules by `CandidateScanTest`, the grid read's by `GridReadTest`, the coverage conditions by `MicroQRCoverageConditionTest` and `SubPixelFrameDecodeTest`, and the budget by `RmQRCoverageBudgetTest`. The corners' rules are caught by `DestinationContractTest`'s skip tests, by timing alone: each failing case measured at least 2.8 times the bound in one run. The terminal returns are caught by `DestinationContractTest`. Each terminal return it catches only by timing was run three times and caught each time, by at least 1.4 times the bound. The smallest margin is rMQR's frame loop on the stacked R13x27 render, and the next smallest is 1.76.
- Not caught:
  - **Micro QR's perspective search, and the arbitrary-orientation path after it.** With the fault, the rest of the search, or of the path within its budget, runs before the read too long is reported.
  - **The perimeter traced in an rMQR outline frame.** With the fault, the outline's remaining frames are traced before the check at the candidate sees the read too long.
  - **rMQR's perspective search's caller and its unrefined fallback: equivalent faults.** The search runs only once the frame got past its format information, which skips the fallback, and the frame then returns its best result, the read too long.
- The timing rules compare the median of calls with a destination of 2 characters against the median of sized calls. The two kinds of call alternate, so that a stall of the machine affects only one call. The bounds are 3 or 5 times, each set against the regression it guards. Each render meant to read through one grid site was found by planting that site's fault. Nothing asserts which site the render reads through, since no result reports the site. The skip renders cover sites too: rMQR's frame loop and module boundaries are caught only on them. So the faults are planted again whenever any of these renders change (`SymbolsToTime`, `SkipImages`, `TwoSkipImages`). Elsewhere the test uses a deterministic observable: a crafted two-text image, or the skip's premise asserted per case.

**Residuals**
- A false finder candidate outside the symbol that read is still searched in full after a read that did not fit. Revisit if a caller probing its buffer size meets one.
- A symbol that fits, beside one too long for the destination that the strided scan reads, is not read when only the full sweep finds it, since the sweep does not run after that read. A probe drew a small symbol, turned and anti-aliased, below a large one too long for the destination (2026-10-01):
  - an M2 at 1.4 to 2 px/module below an M4: 36 of 144 calls returned the read too long, and 26 of them read the M2 with the sweep run after it;
  - an R7x43 at 1.4 to 2.5 px/module below an R13x99: 12 of 144, all 12 read with the sweep run.

  Revisit if a caller probing its buffer size on an image of several symbols meets one.
- A symbol of the opposite polarity, beside one too long for the destination, is not read, since the inverted pass does not run after a terminal result.
- A symbol whose content fails after the segment decoders' buffer check reads as too long for a destination shorter than its text, where a sized call reports the failure. Such a failure is a payload value out of range, a Kanji cell with no mapping, or a later segment that does not decode. The read too long is terminal, so it also ends the scan and the passes.
- rMQR measured noise frames that report a read too long for the destination with nothing in the image; the residual and when to revisit it are in its record ([rmqr-decoder.md](rmqr-decoder.md#decisions)).

### Package architecture

Since 2.0.0 the library ships as three NuGet packages built from two assemblies in this repository (the core split, 2026-09):

| Package | Assembly | Contents | Depends on |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FeatherQR` | `FeatherQR.dll` | Generators, decoders, data types, options, segmentation, `ModuleRect` geometry, the luminance kernels | Nothing on net8.0 and net10.0; `System.Memory` (netstandard2.0) and `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe` (netstandard2.1) |
| `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` | `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp.dll` | `SymbolRenderer`, the `SKCanvas` extensions, the image builders, `IconData` and shapes, `SKBitmap` decoding as extension members on the core decoders | `FeatherQR`, `SkiaSharp` |
| `SkiaSharp.QrCode` | none | An empty compatibility metapackage: the ID the library shipped under through 1.x keeps restoring | `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` |

Namespaces follow the packages: `FeatherQR` and `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`, with the internals of each under `FeatherQR.Internals` and `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp.Internals`. The former `SkiaSharp.QrCode.Image` sub-namespace is merged into `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`. One namespace per package is the simplest shape to explain in a major version that changes every `using` line anyway.

**Dependency rules.**

- The core references no package other than BCL shims, and those only where the framework lacks `Span<T>`, `ArrayPool<T>` and `Unsafe`. Two guards enforce this. `CoreAssemblyDependencyTest` reads the core assembly's references from metadata for every target framework, and `tools/check_package_deps.cs` reads the packed nuspecs (see "Package graph" below). A dependency that slips in passes the build and the tests, but fails both guards.
- The rendering package uses the core through its public surface, plus the `InternalsVisibleTo` uses listed below ("Package seam"). The core never references the rendering package.
- Skia types appear only in the rendering assembly. Inside `namespace FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`, the simple name `SkiaSharp` resolves to that namespace. So `using SkiaSharp;` goes above the file-scoped namespace declaration, and qualified spellings such as `SkiaSharp.SKBitmap` are not used.
- No unified `Create(symbology, ...)` entry point is ever added. The three generators, decoders and data types do not reference each other, and that is what makes trimming precise: a consumer that uses one symbology keeps one symbology.

**What the split buys, measured.** With `PublishTrimmed` (`TrimMode=full`) on a console app, measured on 2026-09-04 on the pre-split assembly:

| Consumer profile | Trimmed managed assembly |
|---:|---:|
| QR encode only | 95 KB |
| All three symbologies, encode | 153 KB |
| All three, encode and decode, including `TryDecode(SKBitmap)` | 229 KB |
| Untrimmed net10.0 | 384 KB |

The managed assembly was never the cost. `libSkiaSharp` is 11.9 MB per RID, cannot be trimmed, and is deployed whether or not a single Skia call survives trimming. Only a package boundary removes it, and only for consumers that reference `FeatherQR` alone. A per-symbology package split was rejected. It would save untrimmed consumers roughly 100 to 130 KB, but it would need a four-package core with a public surface for the shared kernels, and it would gain nothing for trimmed consumers, who already get the numbers above.

**What "lightweight" means.** The brand word is defined as zero dependencies in the core, zero allocations on the hot paths, and trim and NativeAOT safety. It is not a claim about assembly bytes. At 300 to 390 KB the core is larger than single-symbology libraries, because it contains three symbologies, the decoders and the SIMD tiers. The README states the definition in its first lines, so the name never has to be defended against a byte count.

### Package seam: what the rendering package reaches through `InternalsVisibleTo`

`FeatherQR` grants `InternalsVisibleTo` to `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`. The rule is that a third-party renderer must be possible to write against the public surface alone. So every internal that the first-party renderer still uses is listed here, with either its public replacement or the reason it stays internal. The list is checked by building the rendering project with the grant removed: whatever fails to compile is the list.

| Internal | Used by | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| `LuminanceConverter.Convert(pixels, width, height, rowBytes, PixelLayout, premultipliedAlpha, luminance)`, `PixelLayout`, `ImageDimensions.TryGetPixelCount` | `Internals.BitmapLuminanceConverter` and the `SKBitmap` decode overloads | **Stays internal, by decision (core split Phase 2).** The public decode seam is `TryDecodeImage(luminance, width, height, ...)`, which already lets a third-party adapter decode from any image library. Such an adapter does not get the SIMD conversion and the white-compositing behavior for free, and no such adapter has been asked for. Publishing the kernels cannot be undone (removing an API needs a major version, adding one needs a minor), so they stay internal until a concrete request exists. The `TryDecodeImage` documentation states the white-compositing expectation, so that a hand-written converter does not composite transparent pixels against black. The rendering package keeps a single-entry adapter, `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp.Internals.BitmapLuminanceConverter` (`SKColorType` to `PixelLayout` over `SKPixmap.GetPixelSpan()`), so promoting the seam later is a visibility change, not a redesign |
| `RmQRConstants.QuietZoneModules`, `RmQRConstants.IsValidVersion` | `RmQRCodeImageBuilder` | **Replaced.** The builder takes the specified quiet zone from `default(RmQRCodeGeneratorOptions).QuietZoneSize`, the same constant behind a public property. It validates a requested version with `Enum.IsDefined`, which is exact because the `RmQRVersion` enum is contiguous |
| `IModuleMatrixView`, `StandardQrMatrixView` / `MicroQRMatrixView` / `RmQRMatrixView`, `ModuleRunEnumerator<TView>` | `SymbolRenderer` merged-run and per-module drawing loops | **Stays internal, by decision.** The public equivalent is `GetModuleRectangles` / `TryGetModuleRectangles` on the three data types, built on the same `ModuleRunScanner`, so a third-party renderer draws exactly the geometry the first-party one does. The first-party renderer keeps the streaming enumerator, because it draws each run as it finds it, with no rectangle buffer. Going through the public surface would add a rental of `GetModuleRectanglesMaxCount()` size per render (up to ~15,700 rectangles for version 40) to the one path that is measured as allocation-free. Exposing the struct-generic view machinery itself would freeze an implementation detail as API for one caller |

### Package graph: what each nuspec declares

Three packages ship from one `dotnet pack`, all at one shared version (`Directory.Build.props`): `FeatherQR` (core), `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` (rendering, depends on `FeatherQR` and `SkiaSharp`) and `SkiaSharp.QrCode` (an empty compatibility metapackage that depends on `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` and has no `lib/`). After every pack in CI, `tools/check_package_deps.cs` opens the packed nupkgs and asserts the exact dependency group of every target framework. The expected graph is a literal table in the tool, so a change to the graph is a diff someone accepts on purpose.

**The core is dependency-free where the framework carries `Span<T>`, `ArrayPool<T>` and `Unsafe`, and depends on the BCL shims where it does not.** The net8.0 and net10.0 groups are empty. netstandard2.0 depends on `System.Memory`, and netstandard2.1 on `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe`. Before the split these came in transitively through SkiaSharp, which is why removing SkiaSharp broke only the netstandard builds. "Zero dependencies" in the package description means this.

**Transitive pinning is off for the whole repository.** `CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled` writes every transitive package that has a `PackageVersion` entry into the nuspec as a direct dependency. For 1.x that meant `SkiaSharp.NativeAssets.Win32` and `.macOS` beside `SkiaSharp`. In the metapackage it would have meant `SkiaSharp` and the native assets beside `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`. The promotion changes nothing a consumer resolves (SkiaSharp brings its native assets itself). But it makes the package declare a graph it does not have, and it makes the assertion above meaningless. The other half of the feature, forcing a minimum transitive version on applications, has no use here. The test, benchmark, playground and sample projects are not shipped products, `NuGetAudit` reports a vulnerable resolution, and a direct `PackageReference` raises a transitive version whenever one needs raising. So one setting in `Directory.Packages.props` is simpler than a per-project exception that every future packable project would have to remember.

### Public API direction

Each symbology gets its own generator entry point with symbology-typed version and error-correction parameters.

**One naming rule decides every public name in both packages.** A prefix says which symbology a type belongs to (`QR` for Standard QR, `MicroQR`, `RmQR`), and no prefix means the type is shared by all three. A noun that literally means *a code* keeps the `{Sym}Code` form (`QRCodeData`, `MicroQRCodeGenerator`, `RmQRCodeDecodeInfo`). Everything else (enums, ranges and strategies) takes the short prefix (`QREccLevel`, `QRSegmentation`, `QRVersionRange`). Three-letter acronyms are Pascal-cased (`Ecc`, `Eci`, `Bom`).

The rule was implicit while Micro QR and rMQR were built, which is why those two already followed it. 2.0.0 applied it to the Standard QR types written first (`ECCLevel`, `QRCodeSegmentation`, `QRCodeVersionRange`). It also applied it to the shared types that had taken the `QRCode` prefix while meaning the whole family: `QRCodeDecodeStatus` became `DecodeStatus`, and in the rendering package `QRCodeRenderer` and `QRCodeImageBuilderBase<TSelf>` became `SymbolRenderer` and `SymbolImageBuilderBase<TSelf>`, using the word both standards use. The defect the rule removes is that double meaning: `QRCode` cannot mean Standard QR in one type name and the whole family in the next. `QRCodeExtensions` became `SKCanvasExtensions`, following the neighbouring BCL habit of naming an extension class after what it extends.

**The method name repeats what the class already says, so it says nothing.** Since 2.0.0, `QRCodeGenerator.CreateQrCode`, `MicroQRCodeGenerator.CreateMicroQRCode` and `RmQRCodeGenerator.CreateRmQRCode` are all `Create`. That also removes, rather than answers, the `Qr` versus `QR` casing question those method names raised, which is why the rule needs no clause about it.

**Options live in a per-symbology options struct, and since 2.0.0 that is the only way to configure a generator.** `QRCodeGeneratorOptions`, `MicroQRCodeGeneratorOptions` and `RmQRCodeGeneratorOptions` are `readonly record struct`s passed by `in`, so the allocation-free entry points stay allocation-free. The parameter-list overloads released in 1.1.1 were frozen through 1.2.0 (exact signatures, exceptions and messages, never another parameter) and removed in 2.0.0. rMQR never had them.

The rule exists because the parameter-list shape had already failed on rMQR before it shipped. It had reached 10 methods with up to 9 parameters, and one option had leaked into method names. `EciMode` could not be added as a positional parameter without disturbing the existing order, so `CreateRmQRCodeWithEci` and two siblings were added instead. That doubled the method count, while Standard QR expressed the same concept as an ordinary parameter.

**The reshaping was possible only because of a release window.** No rMQR API had ever been in a NuGet package, so its surface could be fixed by deletion at no compatibility cost. Standard QR and Micro QR had no such freedom, and kept their released overloads. Package validation against the last published package enforced the difference (`EnablePackageValidation` with `PackageValidationBaselineVersion`). The baseline then stayed at 1.1.1 for the rest of the 1.x line instead of moving with each release, so the surface that 1.2.0 added was never covered by a baseline. The baseline is unset on the 2.0.0 packages until 2.0.0 ships. A minor release cannot reopen that window. The 2.0.0 major version is what let the deprecation cycle finish, and any change of the same kind waits for the next major.

**Package validation only polices the half of a change that breaks somebody, so the exported surface is also held to a listing in the repository.** Validation answers "would this break a caller who compiled against the last release?", and a new public member never does. Without the listing, a new member would land unreviewed, which is the wrong default for a library whose next release is a rename. `src/FeatherQR/PublicAPI.approved.txt` and `src/FeatherQR.SkiaSharp/PublicAPI.approved.txt` record every exported type and member of the two assemblies. `tools/check_public_api.cs` regenerates them, and the check gates pull requests and runs again at release.

A listing only catches what it prints. Until 2026-09-13 properties were listed without `abstract` / `virtual` / `override`. So when `FinderPatternShape.RequiresAntialiasing` became abstract, which stops an already-compiled subclass from loading, the check passed it as "unchanged". That lasted until the same helper was used for both accessors and methods. Changing the surface is therefore a diff someone accepts deliberately, and the 2.0.0 reshaping arrives as one reviewable file rather than as a claim in a pull request description.

**On a builder option, `null` means the option is absent and never "the default value".** A default that has a name is passed by name: `RectangleModuleShape.Default` and `RectangleFinderPatternShape.Default` for plain shapes, and `SKColors.Black` and `SKColors.White` for the two colours. Through 2.0.0-preview.2 the fluent setters also accepted `null` for those states. That gave a second spelling to a state that already had one. It also let `WithColors`'s optional parameters look like "leave the rest alone" while they behaved as "reset the rest": appending `.WithColors(clearColor: …)` to a chain discarded the colours an earlier call had set. 2.0.0 made the colours and both shape setters non-nullable. It cut `WithColors` down to the two colours a symbol always has, both required, and added `WithCodeColor` / `WithBackgroundColor` / `WithClearColor` so that one colour can be changed on its own. The nulls that remain mean an absence rather than a value: no gradient, no icon, and no clear colour of its own, in which case the padding follows the background.

**The rule is about a default that stands in for a value, not about optional parameters as such.** `WithModuleShape(shape, sizePercent = 1.0f)` and `WithFormat(format, quality = 100)` were reviewed against it on 2026-09-14 and left as they are. Their defaults are the values themselves, written in the signature and in the parameter documentation, so omitting the argument does what it appears to do. A second call to either setter replaces the first, rather than adjusting it.

**`WithFinderPatternShape` was the row that had to be measured rather than reasoned about, and the first measurement was too narrow.** Omitting it is not the same code path as naming the square. Without it, the finders are drawn with the modules, and `RectangleFinderPatternShape.Default` is substituted only once the modules are styled (the rule that styling never reaches a finder pattern). So omitting it looked like a third state, *auto*. In raster output the two spellings are pixel-identical across symbologies, canvas sizes and background alphas. They once differed, invisibly: by one step of one channel, in tens of pixels, under a gradient over a translucent background, because the finder pass composited through a layer and the merged-run path did not. With the layer gone (recorded below) they are 0 pixels apart there too, measured at 300 to 900 pixels square. So the null was a second spelling of a named value, and the merged-run path is an implementation detail the builder keeps for callers who never ask for a shape.

In SVG the two spellings are still not element-identical, and cannot be. Naming the square sends the finders through the finder pass, which writes five rectangles for each. Omitting it leaves them to the merged-run path, which writes thirty elements more on Standard QR at every alpha. Until the finder drawing changed (below), the defect was that the documents also *looked* different. The equivalence claim is about pixels, and applies to raster and SVG alike; it is not about the element list.

The `SKCanvas.Render` extensions keep `null` for every option, and `SymbolRenderer.Render` keeps it for every option except the two colours. For the shapes, and for every parameter of the extensions, the reason is the language rather than the rule. A C# optional parameter needs a constant default, and a shape instance is not a constant. `SKColor` has no constant spelling for black, and `default` is transparent. That was not the reason for `SymbolRenderer.Render`'s `codeColor` and `backgroundColor`, which were *required* parameters typed `SKColor?`. Only consistency with the extensions that forward to them kept those nullable. Their documentation showed that the pair was never revisited: it described them as omittable until the 2.0.0 review corrected it. Since 2026-09-13 they are `SKColor`, and the extensions resolve an omitted colour to black or white before forwarding, as they already did for the clear colour.

The other candidate was a colourless overload beside each of the three, defaulting to black on white. It was compiled before being declined. It binds every positional and named spelling unambiguously except `default, default`. But on Standard QR, the only overload with an `IconData?` parameter, it lets the old `Render(canvas, area, data, null, null)` compile by taking the two nulls as `iconData` and `moduleShape`. The result is pixel-identical and undiagnosed, so the compiler could no longer hand that migration to the caller. Micro QR and rMQR would refuse the same call, since the second `null` would have to reach a `float`. The overload lost on the caller's experience rather than on that. The `SKCanvas` a caller holds never assumes a colour, since every Skia draw call takes its paint. Omission already exists one layer up, in both the builders and the extensions. And a second signature per symbology is one more to keep in step for every option added later.

Under a gradient, a caller now writes a code colour that is not used. That is `SKPaint`'s own model, where a shader takes precedence over the colour. The parameter documentation says so, and gives the two cases where the colour is painted after all: a gradient whose direction is `None`, and no gradient. A fill type that would make the two exclusive was designed and declined on 2026-09-14. The builders have to keep the colour and the gradient as two states, for a caller that chooses between them at run time. So only the static surface would have taken the fill, and the two surfaces would have modelled the same thing differently.

For the colours and the module shape, the rule changed what a caller can write and nothing about the output, since the renderer already resolved each `null` to exactly the values the builder now holds. Until the finder drawing changed (below), the finder shape was the one case where the *substitute* a caller reaches for, rather than the rule itself, could change the output, and only in SVG.

**A finder shape draws its dark modules only; the light ring is a hole, never a paint and never an erase.** Until 2.0.0 a `FinderPatternShape` drew the outer square dark and then painted the ring light over it. That is wrong on any background below alpha 255: the ring came out as a translucent light over dark. So the renderer wrapped each finder in a `SaveLayer` and let the shape erase the ring with `SKBlendMode.Clear`. That is correct on a raster surface, but `SKSvgCanvas` cannot express it and dropped the whole layer. The SVG document had no finder patterns at all, a symbol nothing can scan. This happened on every symbology and by two routes: an explicit `WithFinderPatternShape`, and any styled module set (styling substitutes a solid square finder). The condition was exactly `background alpha < 255`; 254 was enough. It was measured before the change with this library's own decoder, on browser-rasterised SVG of Standard QR at 512x512. The four non-opaque cases (alpha 254 and 128 with a named square, alpha 128 and 0 with styled modules) all failed, and the two opaque ones read.

The fix is geometry rather than erasure. The ring is a hole in what the shape draws, so it shows whatever the renderer already put beneath it, which is the background at any alpha. There is no layer and no blend mode, and both canvas kinds get the same drawing.

**Which geometry expresses the hole is decided by what `SKSvgCanvas` can write**, since it flattens a path into thousands of quadratic segments but writes a rectangle or an oval as one element. So the square finder is four bands and a centre rectangle. A circle's ring is a one-module stroke of its middle oval, with the centre a filled oval. The stroke covers exactly the region between the 5x5 and 7x7 ovals, because a circle's offset curve is another circle. The two rounded shapes need an even-odd path for their ring, whose radii differ per contour, but keep any oval centre out of that path. Measured on a 512x512 Standard QR of "https://githu" at ECC M, 29 modules (the figures move with the module count), a circle finder's document is 5.8 KB drawn this way against 49.9 KB as one even-odd path, and the rounded-circle one is 35.7 KB against 50.4 KB. The stroke works only where the cells are square, because one stroke width cannot be one module on both axes. So a shape handed a non-square rect falls back to the path; the renderer never hands it one.

The two `Draw` overloads that took a light colour or paint were removed with the layer, since a shape that painted the ring could only be made right by erasing. The contract is now the one method, which draws dark modules only. In the same change, the finder's antialiasing started following the finder shape rather than the module shape, so a square finder beside round modules stays crisp. `RequiresAntialiasing` is `abstract`, as `ModuleShape`'s is, because the renderer now sets antialiasing from it in both directions, and an inherited default would silently mean "draw my curves aliased". The lesson is the one the rule above already states from the decoder's side. A finder pattern is read as runs of dark and light, and the light runs are the background, so they should be drawn as the background and not as a colour that has to match it.

**The listing is read from every target framework, which turned an assumption into a fact.** The library builds for four target frameworks, and nothing had ever compared them. The claim that no exported member is framework-conditional existed only in a tool comment. It was true when the gate was introduced, and a build where it stops being true now fails instead of shipping. Two renderers of the same surface exist on purpose: the reflection one behind the Playground's API page, and the metadata one behind the gate. Because the two must agree line for line, neither can drift unnoticed.

An options type is named `{consuming generator}Options`, mechanically, so no reader has to work out which struct belongs to which generator. This follows the BCL habit of naming an options type after its consumer (`JsonSerializerOptions` for `JsonSerializer`), and leaves `{X}DecoderOptions` free under the same rule.

Consequences worth stating here rather than three times:

- **The `options` parameter carries a default on every entry point, and could not while the parameter lists existed.** rMQR had `in RmQRCodeGeneratorOptions options = default` from the start, because its parameter-list versions were deleted before release. On Standard QR and Micro QR a defaulted options parameter would have made `Create(text, ecc)` ambiguous between the two sets of overloads. So callers wrote `QRCodeGeneratorOptions.Default with { ... }` explicitly until 2.0.0 removed the other set. Sizing never had the problem: `TryGetRequiredBufferSize` was always the only sizing overload, so its options parameter was defaulted from the start. The asymmetry came from the released surface rather than from a preference, which is why removing that surface was enough to end it.

- **`default(T)` must be the complete default configuration**, since it is what an omitted argument passes. A member whose documented default is not the zero value stores an offset from that default, not a `value + 1` sentinel. Then writing the default explicitly produces the same value as not writing it, and the generated equality does not report two identical option sets as different. `QuietZoneSize` is the only such member today. Its correct default differs per symbology (4, 2, 2), which is also why one shared options type cannot express it.
- **Options are not shared across symbologies.** The only member the three option sets have in common is one `int` with three different correct defaults. `Version` is a different type in each, Micro QR has no ECI, and rMQR's fit options mean nothing elsewhere. A shared type would carry members invalid for two thirds of its uses, and reject them at run time instead of at compile time.
- **The error correction level stays a required parameter and is deliberately not an option.** It is the only input with no correct default. L and H differ by roughly 4x in capacity, and choosing between capacity and robustness is the caller's decision, not the library's. Putting it in the options struct would force `default(T)` to make that choice silently, which contradicts the rule above. The line this draws: the required arguments say *what symbol you want* (the text and how robust it must be), and the options say *how to encode and render it*. The image builders do default it to `M`, which is right for a "just give me a picture" entry point and wrong for the generator.
- **A version *range* exists only where versions are totally ordered.** `QRVersionRange` (1-40) and `MicroQRVersionRange` (M1-M4) also express the single requested version: a pinned version is the degenerate `Exactly` case. `null` and `int?` convert implicitly, so an optional version needs no branch at the call site. rMQR has no range because its 32 versions have no min/max relation, and it constrains the fit with `RmQRFitStrategy` and `RmQRHeight` instead.

**The `string` convenience overloads went with them.** `string` converts implicitly to `ReadOnlySpan<char>`, so `Create("text", ecc)` still binds to the span overload. All the overloads added was a parameter name (`plainText` rather than `textSpan`) and a second row in every IntelliSense list. They were kept while their released counterparts fixed the shape, and dropped with them in 2.0.0. That also ended the asymmetry where only Standard QR had a `string` destination overload. Every generator now has two `Create` methods, span and span-plus-destination, plus `TryGetRequiredBufferSize`.

That reasoning was recorded as true on all four target frameworks, and it is true on three. The conversion is synthesized by the compiler; it is not an operator on `System.String`. When `ReadOnlySpan<T>` comes from the `System.Memory` package instead of the framework, only C# 14 synthesizes it. That is the case for the netstandard2.0 asset, which is what .NET Framework consumers bind to. Every language version through 13 reports `CS1503` there. The lesson is that "converts implicitly" depends on where the span type comes from and on the consumer's compiler, not on the target framework. A claim about consumer compilation has to be measured from a consumer project. Reasoning from the library's own build proves nothing, because the library compiles at C# 14.

The same measurement found the larger problem. `init` accessors need C# 9, so on the netstandard2.0 (default C# 7.3) and netstandard2.1 (default C# 8.0) assets the option structs could not be configured at all once the parameter lists were gone. Each of the three, and `IconData`, now has a constructor for those consumers. That is why the shape tests treat an option settable only through an object initializer as a defect.

Decoding: matrix-level entry points name their symbology explicitly. Matrix size alone distinguishes Micro QR 11–17 from Standard 21–177, but rectangular input needs width and height. Image-level decoding keeps Standard-QR-only scanning as the default. The other symbologies are opt-in, so the existing detection hot path keeps its performance characteristics.

**A successful image decode also says where the symbol was.** Every `*DecodeInfo` carries `Corners`, a `SymbolCorners` of four `ImagePoint`s (both shared, library-built record structs). They are the outer corners of the module area, quiet zone excluded, in the input's *continuous* pixel coordinates: (0, 0) is the top-left corner of the top-left pixel, so the values plot directly in SkiaSharp, a canvas or System.Drawing. No shift is applied at the boundary. The finder centres that every mapping is anchored on come from run boundaries with an exclusive end, and are already in that convention, so a symbol drawn from pixel 48 reports 48.0. The first implementation added half a pixel, on the theory that the samplers' `(int)(x + 0.5f)` meant "integer = pixel centre"; a tenth-of-a-pixel test on the finder-anchored corners is what caught it.

The corners are named in the symbol's own frame: `TopLeft` is beside the finder that defines the symbol's top-left, wherever the camera put it. That is what lets one quadrilateral report rotation and, through reversed winding, mirroring. The square decoders retry a mirrored capture by transposing the sampled matrix, so the one bit they have to report is whether that retry won. rMQR's frames swap axes instead, and its transform is already in symbol order. The value is set only on `Success`: a matrix decode has no image, and a failed image decode located nothing a caller should draw.

It is an estimate from the fitted geometry, and the stated bound depends on how much each decoder infers. Standard QR fits from three finders plus an alignment pattern, and on the mesh path uses a transform re-anchored on the mesh's far lattice node. It stays within half a module for flat, rotated, mirrored and keystoned captures at the tilts the corner tests run, **and at 8 px per module or more**. The tilts are 12 % on versions 2 and 5, 6 to 8 % on 7 and 10, and 5 to 6 % from version 14 up. The 8 px per module test scene decodes further on most versions, to 15 to 17 % on 2 and 5 and 10 % on 7 and 30, and stays within the bound there too.

Below that density the bound is better stated in pixels than in modules. The bottom-right corner is anchored on the alignment pattern, whose centre the finder resolves to roughly a pixel at any module size. So the error is nearly constant in pixels (measured on version 2 over every rotation: 4.09 px at 6 px per module, 3.63 at 8, 3.94 at 12), while the module it is divided by shrinks: 0.68 module at 6 px per module against 0.33 at 12. These were measured before the alignment centre was refined to a fraction of a pixel on images with grey levels (2026-09-25), and not measured since.

A second loosening is structural rather than a matter of scale. Whenever the bottom-right alignment pattern is not located, `BuildGridTransform` falls back to the finders-only parallelogram quad that version 1 always gets, and error correction still returns `Success`. So a symbol of version 2 or up with one damaged module over that pattern reports an ordinary result, with that corner up to about a module and a half out. The public contract states both limits, because nothing in `QRCodeDecodeInfo` tells a caller which fit ran.

Micro QR and rMQR fit from a single finder, and stay within half a module flat and at right angles (rMQR also at the one oblique angle tested). Beyond that:
- An oblique Micro QR rotation is reported at whichever 1° axis angle decodes first. The finder sweep's run-length score is flat for ±3 to 4° around the true angle, so the winner is routinely 1 to 2° off, and the far corners measure 0.2 to 0.9 module at any pixel scale.
- A Micro QR keystone through the same search measures 0.55 to 0.76 module at 5 to 8 %, and 1.03 mirrored at 8 %.
- An rMQR grid anchored on the sub-finder reads a keystone through error correction without following it, so its far corners carry the residual. At 8 px per module over every version (re-measured 2026-09-28), they measure 1.27 module with the top edge shortened 2 % a side, 1.55 to 1.86 at 3 to 8 % (worst R17x43), and 2.10 at 10 % (R11x27). With the left edge shortened to 4 %, they measure 0.67 or less. The stronger keystones, which only a grid traced round the symbol's perimeter reads, measure 0.16 or less with the left edge shortened, and 0.59 and 0.47 with the top shortened 12 and 15 %.

The contract says "about a module" for those, and "about two modules" for an rMQR symbol from 2 % up. At 2 %, 7 of 32 versions are over a module, so the threshold is 2 %, and it is not confined to short symbols. Tightening these bounds means tracing the winning grid's perimeter after a read, a follow-up in [rmqr-decoder.md](rmqr-decoder.md). `System.Numerics.Vector2` was not used because on netstandard2.0 it would add a package dependency to a package that advertises none. No reference library returns this for Standard QR, which is why it was worth a public type.

Image builders: one builder per symbology, all deriving from `SymbolImageBuilderBase<TSelf>`, a self-referential generic, so fluent chains keep the concrete type. The base holds every shared option and the complete raster and SVG output surface. A symbology builder adds only its typed options (ECC, version), and connects its data model through three `private protected` hooks. Two guards keep the surfaces from drifting apart. The base class makes it structurally impossible to leave out an output method. `QrImageBuilderApiParityTest` (reflection over the public surfaces, with a documented list of allowed differences) catches asymmetry in what cannot be shared, the symbology-typed static helpers. The rMQR builder extends the same base and is covered by the same parity test.

Capacity pricing overflow: Byte mode costs `8 × length` bits, so a data length past `int.MaxValue / 8` wraps negative and looks like a fit. All three selectors compute the cost in `long`, including the UTF-8 BOM's `+ 3`, which wraps on its own near `int.MaxValue`. Widening, rather than rejecting the length up front, is a deliberate choice. A length fast path placed ahead of the remaining checks answers "does not fit" for what is actually an argument error. One placed ahead of the Micro QR version check also handed an unvalidated version to the table-indexing error builder. The overflow is reachable only with a quarter-gigabyte input, so `CapacityOverflowGuardTest` calls the selectors directly instead of allocating one.

Sizing: every generator exposes exactly one sizing method, `TryGetRequiredBufferSize`, with one contract across all three symbologies: `false` means the content does not fit, and argument errors throw. Standard QR and Micro QR kept an `[Obsolete]` throwing `GetRequiredBufferSize` through 1.2.0, only because v1.1.1 had released it, and removed it in 2.0.0. `SizingSurfaceTest` asserts that it is absent rather than assuming it, because a throwing convenience is the kind of thing someone re-adds in good faith. The reasoning is recorded once, in [rmqr-encoder.md](rmqr-encoder.md), including why this is a `Try` overload rather than a dedicated exception type, and why undefined enum values are not folded into `false`. The other two symbologies follow it rather than restating it.

Exact API names and shapes are finalized per-symbology at implementation time, spec-first, following the API-driven development principle in [DESIGN.md](../DESIGN.md).

### Data model direction

`QRCodeData` stays Standard-QR-only. New symbologies get their own data types, with rectangular dimensions (width ≠ height) decided once when the first new type is introduced.

Serialization: the `QRR` format is frozen as-is for Standard QR (header + 1-byte size, sizes 21–177, square). New symbologies use a new serialization header carrying symbol type, width, and height. Old readers reject new-format streams cleanly (the existing header/size validation already guarantees this).

**A value the library hands back is a `readonly record struct` with an internal constructor and get-only properties.** Since 2.0.0, `QRCodeCalculatedSize`, `MicroQRCodeCalculatedSize`, `RmQRCodeCalculatedSize` and the three `*DecodeInfo` types all follow it. Before, Standard QR's sizing result had a public constructor, `init` setters and an `IsValid` property, while the other two were plain structs, and the drift went unnoticed until someone read all three files side by side. The rule follows from what the type is *for*. It is an `out` parameter of a `Try` method, so there is no half-built instance to pass back in. `init` would let a caller edit an answer the library computed. And `IsValid` duplicated the `bool` the `Try` already returned. Only positional records deconstruct, so declaring these without positional parameters drops deconstruction and keeps everything else (`ToString`, `==` and `IEquatable<T>`). Those are what a caller logging a size or comparing two decode results actually uses. `TypeShapeTest` asserts the shape rather than trusting the next type to copy it.

**Being library-built is not a reason to be opaque, and that took two attempts.** The first attempt demoted these to plain structs, which also lost the generated printing and the non-boxing equality: `size.ToString()` returned the type name, and `Equals` started boxing both operands. What had to go was the public constructor and the `init` setters; the record was never the problem. The same mistake hit `GradientOptions` in the same change, where dropping the record silently removed `with`. One rule came out of it: when a type's shape is wrong, identify the member that is wrong and remove that, rather than changing what kind of type it is.

**The three decode results report the same members under the same names**, with two documented exceptions. rMQR has no `MaskPattern`, because ISO/IEC 23941 defines a single data mask. Only Standard QR has `StructuredAppend`, because neither other standard defines it or has a mode indicator for it. Sizing is the same, except that rMQR is rectangular (`Width`/`Height`) and the square symbologies report one `Size`.
